# Appendix B: Answers to Review Questions

These are model answers to the review questions at the end of each chapter. They are
deliberately concise: each states the essential points and names the section where the
chapter develops them, so that you can check your own answer against the text and not just
against this page. Where a question asks for your own design or opinion, the answer shows
what a strong response contains; other well-reasoned answers are equally valid.

---

## Chapter 1 — Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

**1.** Narrow AI performs one task or a closely related set of tasks; General AI is a
hypothetical system that could perform any intellectual task a human can, transferring
knowledge to entirely new domains. Every deployed system is narrow. For system design this
means scoping each AI component to a defined task, evaluating it against that task's
benchmarks, and expecting it to degrade outside its scope, so the surrounding system must
detect and handle out-of-scope inputs. (Section 1.2)

**2.** Any three of the capabilities in Section 1.3, each with an application. For example:
natural language understanding and generation, used to draft replies to support tickets;
pattern recognition, used to flag fraudulent transactions or read medical images;
recommendation and ranking, used to order products or search results; code generation, used
in development assistants; structured prediction, used to extract fields from invoices.
(Section 1.3)

**3.** Any two limitations from Section 1.4 with a matching strategy, for example:
hallucination, reduced by retrieval augmentation and output validation; lack of persistent
memory, addressed by external memory and stored conversation history; context-window limits,
handled by chunking, summarization and compression; reasoning failures, reduced by
chain-of-thought prompting or reasoning models; distribution shift, caught by continuous
monitoring and addressed by retraining or fine-tuning; adversarial inputs, resisted with
input validation and prompt hardening. (Section 1.4, Table 1.2)

**4.** Because it follows from how generative models work. A language model produces the
most plausible continuation of its input; it does not consult a verified store of facts, so
fluent, confident and false output is a natural product of the mechanism, not a defect in a
particular implementation. That is why every production system needs validation, retrieval
grounding or output verification instead of waiting for hallucination to be fixed.
(Section 1.4)

**5.** A strong answer turns "add AI" into a specified task. Ask what problem it should
solve and for whom; what a good output looks like and how it would be measured; what the
inputs are and where the data comes from; what an error costs and who reviews the output;
what latency and budget apply; what privacy, security and compliance constraints exist; and
what the current process is, so success can be compared with it. The chapter's
Engineering Insights contrast a vague goal with a measurable one, such as classifying
tickets into twelve categories with precision of at least 90%. (Section 1.2; Engineering
Insights)

**6.** The AI Effect is the pattern by which an activity stops being regarded as
intelligent once a machine can do it, as happened with chess after Deep Blue. It makes
progress hard to measure because the goalposts move: each achievement is reclassified as
"not really intelligence," so the field appears never to arrive. The chapter's response is to
judge systems by reliable performance on defined problems instead of by a philosophical
definition. (Section 1.1)

**7.** Training is a large, bounded effort: assembling and cleaning data, running expensive
compute for a period, and evaluating the result. Deployment is continuous: serving many
requests with low latency and high availability, paying for inference on every request,
monitoring quality and drift, handling adversarial inputs, and updating models without
breaking dependents. The misconception that inference is free (Section 1.7) shows why
production cost and operations are a separate engineering discipline, the subject of
Volume IV. (Sections 1.4, 1.7)

## Chapter 2 — History and Evolution of Artificial Intelligence

**1.** Symbolic AI assumed that intelligence could be represented as explicit rules,
logical operations and the manipulation of symbols. It failed to scale because real-world
knowledge is largely implicit and hard to articulate, rules conflict and have exceptions,
new situations fall outside any rule library, and building and maintaining the rules became
prohibitively expensive. Systems such as the General Problem Solver worked on well-defined
puzzles and broke on messy, ambiguous tasks. (Sections 2.2, 2.3)

**2.** Expert systems required knowledge engineers to extract an expert's knowledge in
interviews and write it down as IF-THEN rules. Much expertise is implicit, built from years of
experience and intuition, so it resists being written as rules; rules conflicted and had
exceptions; new cases fell outside the library; and the cost of building and maintaining the
rules grew prohibitive. That barrier is the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. (Section 2.3)

**3.** Both winters followed a gap between what AI had been promised to do and what it
delivered. The first (1974–1980) came when systems could not handle real-world complexity
and the UK's Lighthill Report (1973) concluded that AI had produced no significant practical
applications; the second (1987–1993) came when commercial expert systems proved too costly
to maintain and too brittle, and the LISP-machine market collapsed. The lesson is to judge
current progress by demonstrated capability on real tasks, not by confident predictions,
because the winters were failures of expectation, not of the underlying technology.
(Section 2.4)

**4.** Graphics Processing Units. Designed for games, GPUs are very good at the matrix
multiplications neural-network training requires, and they made training orders of
magnitude faster. (Section 2.6)

**5.** AlexNet, a deep convolutional network trained on GPUs, cut the ImageNet top-5 error
rate from 26.2% to 15.3%, far ahead of the previous state of the art. The size of the margin
settled the argument that deep learning was the path forward, and the major technology
companies built or bought deep-learning teams within a few years. (Section 2.6)

**6.** RNNs and LSTMs process a sequence one step at a time and compress everything seen so
far into a fixed-size hidden state, so they lose distant context and cannot be parallelized
across positions. Transformers use self-attention to attend to every position at once,
capturing long-range dependencies directly and allowing training to be parallelized, which
made much larger datasets and models practical. (Sections 2.6, 2.7)

**7.** Pre-training trains a model on a very large general corpus with a self-supervised
objective, such as BERT's masked-word prediction or GPT's next-token prediction, so it learns
general language patterns. Fine-tuning then trains that pre-trained model further on a
smaller, task-specific dataset to adapt it to a particular task. (Section 2.7)

**8.** Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback trains a model toward human preferences:
human raters compare pairs of outputs, their preferences train a reward model, and the
language model is fine-tuned to maximize that reward. It matters because a raw language
model produces plausible continuations but does not reliably follow instructions or behave
helpfully and safely; RLHF, with instruction fine-tuning, is what made assistants such as
ChatGPT useful. (Section 2.8)

---

## Chapter 3 — Machine Learning Fundamentals

**1.** In traditional programming, a person writes the rules and the computer applies them to
data to produce answers. In machine learning, the computer is given data and, in supervised
learning, the desired answers, and it learns the rules (the model's parameters) from them.
Machine learning suits problems whose rules are too complex, too numerous or too changeable
to write by hand. (Section 3.1)

**2.** Supervised learning learns from input–label pairs, for example classifying emails as
spam or not spam, or predicting a house price. Unsupervised learning finds structure in
inputs without labels, for example clustering customers into segments or reducing
dimensionality. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards received while interacting with an
environment, for example game playing, robot control or aligning language models with human
preferences. (Sections 3.3–3.5)

**3.** Each split has a different job: the training set fits the parameters, the validation
set guides choices such as hyperparameters and early stopping, and the test set gives an
unbiased final estimate of performance on unseen data. If they overlap, the model is scored
on examples it has effectively seen, and the estimate of generalization is inflated.
(Section 3.7)

**4.** When fraud is rare, a model that labels almost everything "not fraud" scores very high
accuracy while missing most fraud, so accuracy hides the failure that matters. Use recall on
the fraud class (the share of fraud caught), together with precision so that false alarms
stay manageable, or the F1 score, and look at the confusion matrix. (Section 3.11; Mistake 2)

**5.** A model can fail in two opposite ways. With high bias it is too simple to capture the
real pattern and underfits, doing badly on training and test data alike. With high variance
it is so flexible that it fits noise in the training data and overfits, doing well in
training and badly on new data. Increasing complexity reduces bias and raises variance, and
regularization does the reverse; the goal is the balance that generalizes, and more data
helps in both directions. (Sections 3.9, 3.10)

**6.** Data leakage occurs when information from the validation or test data, or information
that would not be available at prediction time, influences training, through feature
engineering, preprocessing such as scaling fitted on all the data, or model selection. The
model is then evaluated on information it has partly seen, so its scores look better than
the performance it will achieve in production. (Mistake 3; Section 3.7)

**7.** In self-supervised learning the labels come from the data itself: a language model
learns to predict the next token from the tokens before it, so every position in the text
supplies a training example and no human annotation is needed. Training, loss minimization,
generalization and overfitting still work as in supervised learning; what changes is where the
targets come from, which allows training on very large unlabeled corpora. (Section 3.11,
Engineering Note)

---

## Chapter 4 — Neural Networks

**1.** Without an activation function each layer computes an affine map, and a composition of
affine maps is itself affine: three stacked layers reduce to a single
$\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}'\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}'$. The network can then represent only linear
relationships, however many layers it has, and cannot learn non-linear patterns such as XOR.
Non-linear activations are what let depth add representational power. (Section 4.3)

**2.** Sigmoid squashes its input into (0, 1) and has a derivative of at most 0.25 that
approaches zero when it saturates; ReLU outputs $\max(0, z)$ and has a derivative of exactly 1
for positive inputs. In backpropagation the gradient is multiplied by the activation's
derivative at every layer, so with sigmoid it shrinks exponentially, to about $0.25^{10}$
after ten layers, and early layers barely learn: that is the vanishing gradient problem.
ReLU's unit derivative for positive inputs lets gradients pass through without shrinking,
which largely resolves it in that regime. (Sections 4.3, 4.7)

**3.** Cross-entropy matches the probabilistic interpretation of a classifier's output and,
combined with a sigmoid or softmax output, gives gradients that stay large when the model is
wrong, whereas MSE's gradients become small when the output saturates. Its key property is
that the loss grows without bound as the predicted probability of the true class approaches
zero, so a confident wrong prediction is penalized very heavily and produces a strong
corrective signal. (Section 4.6)

**4.** These are "dead" neurons, the dying ReLU problem. A ReLU neuron whose pre-activations
are consistently negative always outputs zero, its gradient is zero, and its weights stop
updating, so it is permanently switched off. Large learning rates or large negative bias
updates that push the neuron into that region are common causes; Leaky ReLU, which keeps a
small slope for negative inputs, is one remedy. (Section 4.3)

**5.** The forward pass sends the input through every layer, computes the loss, and stores
each layer's pre-activations and activations. The backward pass starts from the gradient of
the loss with respect to the output and applies the chain rule layer by layer, back to the
first. The stored values are needed because each layer's gradient depends on its own
activations and their derivatives; reusing them, instead of recomputing them, is what makes
the gradient computation tractable. (Section 4.7)

**6.** The learning rate sets the size of each parameter update along the negative gradient.
Too high, and updates overshoot, so the loss oscillates or diverges; too low, and training is
very slow or stalls. Adam reduces this sensitivity by adapting the effective learning rate for
each weight from running estimates of the gradient and of the squared gradient, so it copes
with gradients of very different scales and needs little tuning. (Section 4.8)

**7.** The theorem guarantees that a suitable network exists, not that training will find it
or that it is efficient. A single wide layer may need an enormous number of units, while deep
networks learn hierarchical features, each layer building more abstract representations on
the last, and for some functions can represent with exponentially fewer parameters what a
shallow network needs great width to match. (Section 4.9)

**8.** Residual (skip) connections add a layer's input directly to its output,
$\mathbf{a}^{(l)} = f(\mathbf{W}^{(l)}\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(l)}) + \mathbf{a}^{(l-1)}$.
They addressed the degradation problem: deeper plain networks had higher error even on their
training data, an optimization difficulty and not overfitting. The addition gives gradients a
path back to earlier layers that is not repeatedly multiplied by activation derivatives, and
lets each layer learn a change to its input instead of a whole new transformation, which made
networks of 50 to over 150 layers trainable. (Section 4.9)

**9.** The large gap between training and test accuracy means the model is overfitting: it
has memorized its training data instead of learning patterns that generalize. Suitable
interventions include regularization (L2 weight decay or dropout), early stopping on
validation loss, reducing model size, or adding and augmenting training data; monitor
training and validation loss together to see which helps. (Engineering Insights; Section 3.9)

**10.** When features have very different scales, their gradients differ in magnitude by the
same factors, so a single learning rate is too large for some weights and too small for
others; training becomes unstable, oscillates or fails to converge, and large-valued features
dominate. Normalizing inputs to zero mean and unit variance puts features on comparable
scales and makes training far more stable. The unscaled character-count feature that stopped
Dev's network learning is the chapter's example. (Engineering Insights; Mistake 2)

---

## Chapter 5 — Deep Learning

**1.** Representation learning means the model learns the features it needs directly from
raw data, building them up through its layers, instead of relying on features designed by
hand. Traditional feature engineering, such as SIFT or HOG for images, took years of expert
work, was specific to one task and domain, and encoded what engineers believed mattered. The
key advantage of learned representations is generality: the same learning approach transfers
across domains, and representations learned on one task can be reused on others, as transfer
learning does. (Section 5.1)

**2.** A convolutional layer applies the same small filter, with the same weights, at every
position of the input, whereas a fully connected layer gives every input–output connection
its own weight. Sharing cuts the number of parameters dramatically, which reduces computation
and the risk of overfitting, and it builds in a useful inductive bias: a pattern such as a
vertical edge is detected the same way wherever it appears in the image. (Section 5.2)

**3.** A feature map is the output of one filter applied across the whole input: a grid
whose value at each position measures how strongly the filter's pattern is present at that
location. Geometrically, each feature map is a spatial map of where one learned feature, such
as an edge of a particular orientation in early layers or an object part in later ones,
occurs in the input. A layer with 64 filters produces 64 feature maps. (Section 5.2)

**4.** In an RNN trained with backpropagation through time, a gradient travelling from step
$t$ back to step $t-k$ is multiplied by $k$ copies of the same recurrent weight matrix and $k$
activation derivatives, so over long sequences it shrinks exponentially (for example
$0.9^{100} \approx 0.000027$) and the network cannot learn long-range dependencies. In a deep
feedforward network the shrinking happens across layers, each with its own weights; in an RNN
it happens across time steps with the same weights repeated, and its length is set by the
sequence, which makes the problem worse for long inputs. (Section 5.3)

**5.** The forget gate decides what to erase from the cell state; the input gate decides
what new candidate information to write into it; and the output gate decides how much of the
cell state to expose as the hidden state. Because the cell state is updated by a gated
addition, $\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t$,
information and gradients can flow across many steps with little attenuation. (Section 5.4)

**6.** The encoder compressed the whole source sentence into one fixed-size vector, its final
hidden state, and the decoder had to produce the translation from that vector alone, which
lost information on long sentences. Bahdanau attention lets the decoder, at each step, score
every encoder hidden state against its previous state, turn the scores into weights with a
softmax, and use the weighted sum of encoder states as a context vector, so it can focus on
the relevant parts of the source for each output word. (Section 5.5)

**7.** Large labeled datasets such as ImageNet, GPU hardware that made training far faster,
and algorithmic advances such as ReLU, dropout, batch normalization and residual connections.
Each was necessary and none sufficient: data without compute could not be used to train large
networks in reasonable time, compute without data would overfit, and both together still
needed the algorithmic advances to make deep networks train stably. (Section 5.6)

**8.** AlexNet reached a top-5 error of 15.3% against 26.2% for the second-place entry, an
improvement far larger than the incremental gains of the hand-engineered approaches that
preceded it. The size of the jump, achieved by a learned representation instead of
hand-designed features, convinced the field to change direction, and deep learning displaced
earlier approaches in vision, speech and language within a few years. (Section 5.6)

**9.** `model.eval()` switches the network from training mode to inference mode. Dropout is
turned off, so every unit participates and predictions are deterministic, and batch
normalization uses the running statistics accumulated during training instead of the
statistics of the current batch. Without it, predictions are noisy and depend on what else is
in the batch. (Lab, Section 5.2)

**10.** As in Chapter 4, Section 4.9, residual connections add each block's input to its
output, giving gradients a path to early layers that bypasses repeated multiplication by
layer derivatives and letting each block learn a change to its input. This overcomes the
degradation problem, in which deeper plain networks are harder to optimize and have higher
training error, and is what makes a 50-layer network such as ResNet-50 trainable. (Sections
4.9, 5.2)

---

## Chapter 6 — Transformer Architecture

**1.** RNNs process tokens one at a time, so computation cannot be parallelized across the
sequence and training on long sequences is slow; and they pass information through a
fixed-size hidden state, so distant context fades and long-range dependencies are hard to
learn. The Transformer replaces recurrence with self-attention, which relates every position
to every other directly in one step, so long-range dependencies are captured without passing
through a chain of states, and all positions are processed in parallel. (Sections 6.1, 6.9)

**2.** $\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(QK^T / \sqrt{d_k}\right) V$. The
queries $Q$ represent what each position is looking for, the keys $K$ what each position
offers for matching, and the values $V$ the content that is combined. $QK^T$ measures the
similarity of each query to each key; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps those scores in a
reasonable range; the row-wise softmax turns them into weights that sum to one; and the
result is a weighted sum of the values for each query. (Section 6.3)

**3.** Dot products grow with the dimension $d_k$, so for large $d_k$ the scores become very
large, the softmax saturates toward a one-hot distribution, and its gradients become nearly
zero. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the variance of the scores near one regardless of
dimension, preventing saturation and keeping gradients useful during training. (Section 6.3)

**4.** In self-attention the queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence, so
every token attends to every other token in its context. Each token's new representation is a
weighted combination of the value vectors of all tokens, with weights set by how relevant
each is to it, so the same word receives a different representation in different contexts:
"bank" near "river" and "bank" near "loan" end up with different vectors. (Section 6.4)

**5.** Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each with its own
learned projections of the queries, keys and values, then concatenates their outputs and
projects them. A single head computes one weighting per position, while several heads can
specialize in different relationships at once, such as syntactic dependencies, coreference,
positional proximity and semantic similarity, which one wider head would have to blend into
a single set of weights. (Section 6.5)

**6.** Self-attention treats its input as a set: without extra information, permuting the
tokens would permute the outputs identically, so the model would not know word order.
Positional encodings add information about each token's position to its embedding. An RNN
does not need them because it processes tokens in order, so position is implicit in its
sequential computation. (Section 6.6)

**7.** Encoder-only models, such as BERT, read the whole input bidirectionally and suit
understanding tasks such as classification and embeddings. Decoder-only models, such as GPT,
generate text autoregressively with masked self-attention and suit generation and chat.
Encoder-decoder models, such as the original Transformer and T5, encode an input and decode an
output with cross-attention, and suit sequence-to-sequence tasks such as translation and
summarization. (Sections 6.7, 6.8)

**8.** Chinchilla found that many large models were undertrained and that a compute-optimal
model should see roughly 20 training tokens per parameter, $D_{\text{optimal}} \approx 20N$.
In practice, for a fixed compute budget a smaller model trained on more data can outperform a
larger model trained on less, so training decisions should scale data along with parameters,
as later models such as Llama 2 and Mistral did. (Section 6.9)

**9.** Every token attends to every other, so attention's computation and memory grow with
the square of the sequence length: a tenfold increase in context means about a hundredfold
increase in attention cost. That sets a practical ceiling on context length, governed by
compute, memory and cost, and has driven work on more efficient attention and on extending
context; it also means long contexts should be used deliberately, not by default. (Section
6.10)

**10.** Models use information near the beginning and end of a long context more reliably
than information in the middle, so critical content placed mid-context may effectively be
ignored (Liu et al., 2023). When structuring long prompts, put instructions and the most
important information at the beginning or end, keep the context focused, and order retrieved
documents so the most relevant are not buried in the middle. (Section 6.10)

---

## Chapter 7 — Large Language Models

**1.** A word-level vocabulary large enough for real text is enormous, still meets words it
has never seen (names, typos, new terms, other languages), and treats related forms such as
"run" and "running" as unrelated. Character-level models avoid unknown words but produce very
long sequences. BPE solves the problem with subword units: it learns a vocabulary of frequent
character sequences, so common words become single tokens, rare words split into a few
pieces, and any input can be represented, because single characters remain in the vocabulary
as a fallback. (Sections 7.1, 7.2)

**2.** BPE starts from a vocabulary of individual characters (or bytes), counts every
adjacent pair of symbols in the training corpus, merges the most frequent pair into a new
token, and repeats. The number of merge operations, chosen in advance, determines the final
vocabulary size; at inference the learned merges are applied in priority order to split any
input deterministically. (Section 7.2)

**3.** Token embeddings encode semantic meaning, so words with similar meanings have similar
vectors, and syntactic and relational information. The observation that the vector for
"king" minus "man" plus "woman" lands close to "queen" shows that relationships such as
gender are encoded as roughly consistent directions in the space: meaning has a geometry.
(Section 7.3)

**4.** The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can process in one
request, input and output together. A 130,000-token prompt does not fit a 128,000-token
window; depending on the API it is rejected with an error or truncated, losing content. A
production application should count tokens before sending, reserve space for the response,
and reduce the input by priority, through truncation of low-value content, summarization of
history or chunking with retrieval, instead of letting the request fail. (Section 7.4)

**5.** The objective is to maximize $\prod_t P(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1})$, equivalently to
minimize $-\sum_t \log P(x_t \mid x_{<t})$, the next-token cross-entropy over the training
text. Predicting the next token well across a vast and varied corpus requires modeling grammar,
facts, reasoning patterns and document structures such as summaries and translations, because
those all appear in the text; capabilities such as summarization and translation therefore
emerge from the generality of the objective and the data, without being trained directly.
(Section 7.5)

**6.** Temperature 0 makes the model choose the most probable token at every step, so the
same prompt yields near-identical, safe and often repetitive text, which is the opposite of
what creative writing needs. A temperature of about 0.7 to 1.0 keeps the output coherent while
allowing diverse word choices, often combined with nucleus sampling; the right value should be
tuned against what users find engaging. (Section 7.6)

**7.** Top-k samples from the $k$ most probable tokens; nucleus (top-p) sampling samples from
the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds $p$. A fixed $k$ is too
restrictive when the distribution is flat, when many tokens are plausible, and too permissive
when it is peaked, when only a few are. Top-p adapts the size of the candidate pool to the
model's confidence, small when it is sure and large when it is not. (Section 7.7)

**8.** Any two of the chapter's causes, each with a mitigation. The training signal rewards
plausibility, not truth, and the model conflates frequency with truth: ground answers in
retrieved, verified documents and require citations. The model cannot know what it does not
know: build verification layers, and prompt it to express uncertainty. Context pressure
pushes it toward complete, fluent output even without facts, as in a request for a
biography: constrain the task to the provided sources, allow "I don't know," and use low
temperature for factual tasks. (Section 7.8)

**9.** Stage 1, supervised fine-tuning, trains the base model on high-quality demonstrations
so it follows instructions. Stage 2 trains a reward model on human comparisons of pairs of
responses, so it can score outputs by predicted human preference. Stage 3 optimizes the
fine-tuned model with reinforcement learning (PPO) to maximize that reward. The KL-divergence
penalty keeps the optimized model close to the supervised model, which limits reward hacking:
exploiting flaws in the reward model with outputs that score well but are not actually
better. (Section 7.9)

**10.** LoRA freezes the pre-trained weight matrix $W$ and trains a low-rank update
$\Delta W = BA$, where $B$ is $d \times r$ and $A$ is $r \times k$ with $r$ much smaller than
$d$ or $k$, so the trainable parameters fall from $d \times k$ to $r(d + k)$: a 128-fold
reduction for a 4096 × 4096 matrix with $r = 16$. It exploits the observation that the weight
updates learned during fine-tuning tend to have low intrinsic rank. (Section 7.10)

---

## Chapter 8 — Generative AI

**1.** A discriminative model learns $P(y \mid x)$, the probability of a label given an input,
and is used for classification and prediction, drawing boundaries between categories. A
generative model learns $P(x)$, the distribution of the data itself, and so can sample new
examples that resemble the training data, such as text, images or audio. (Section 8.1)

**2.** The forward process takes a real image and adds Gaussian noise over many small steps
until only noise remains; it is fixed and needs no learning. The reverse process removes noise
step by step, starting from pure noise, to produce an image. What the model learns is the
reverse step: given a noisy image and the step number, it predicts the noise to remove, a
small correction that, repeated many times, turns noise into a coherent image. (Section 8.3)

**3.** Latent diffusion runs the diffusion process in a compressed latent space produced by a
trained encoder–decoder (a VAE) instead of on the full pixel grid, and the decoder maps the
final latent back to an image. Because each spatial dimension is compressed by a factor of
about 4 to 16, every denoising step processes far less data, which cuts the computation per
step dramatically and made high-resolution generation feasible on consumer hardware.
(Section 8.3)

**4.** The model generates one token at a time, each conditioned on all the tokens before it,
sampling from its predicted distribution and appending the result until it emits a stop token
or reaches a limit. The joint probability factorizes as
$P(x_1, \ldots, x_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1})$. (Section 8.2)

**5.** Top-k sampling restricts each step to the $k$ most probable tokens and renormalizes over
them; nucleus (top-p) sampling restricts it to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative
probability reaches $p$. Top-k always keeps the same number of candidates, while top-p keeps
few when the model is confident and many when it is uncertain. (Section 8.2)

**6.** Fill-in-the-middle training teaches a model to predict a missing middle segment from
the code before and after it. Code completion usually happens inside an existing file, where
the new code must fit between lines that are already written, so a model that uses both the
prefix and the suffix produces completions that fit their surroundings. (Section 8.6)

**7.** Generated code can look syntactically correct and functionally plausible while
containing vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, missing input validation, buffer overflows,
hardcoded credentials or misused cryptography, and its fluency encourages people to trust it.
Production use therefore needs the same review, testing and security scanning as human code,
or more. (Section 8.6)

**8.** A vision encoder, typically a Vision Transformer, divides an image into patches and
encodes each as an embedding vector, much as a tokenizer turns text into token embeddings.
Those patch embeddings, projected into the language model's embedding space, are combined with
the text embeddings, so the language model attends over image and text together and can
reason about both. (Section 8.7)

**9.** Any three risks with a mitigation each, for example: deepfakes, addressed with
provenance standards such as C2PA, watermarking and detection classifiers; copyright
infringement, addressed with licensing agreements, data governance and output filtering;
bias amplification, addressed with diverse datasets, bias audits and diverse raters; phishing
and fraud, addressed with platform detection and authentication; harmful content, addressed
with safety training, content classifiers and system prompts. (Section 8.8, Table 8.4)

**10.** C2PA, the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, is a standard for
attaching signed provenance records to media files, describing how a file was created and
edited. It addresses the difficulty of telling authentic media from synthetic media, such as
deepfakes, by establishing where content came from instead of trying to detect fakes after
the fact. (Section 8.8)

---

## Chapter 9 — Reasoning Models

**1.** Standard generation commits to each token as it writes, with no separate stage for
working anything out, which suffices when the answer is a retrievable pattern. Multi-step
problems require identifying the relevant relationships, computing intermediate results,
keeping track of state across steps and checking the answer, as in the chapter's two-trains
problem; a model that maps the problem straight to an answer pattern cannot do that reliably.
(Section 9.1)

**2.** Chain-of-thought prompting has the model write out intermediate steps before the
answer. Each written step becomes context for the next, so the model conditions on a richer,
more structured context and in effect uses its own text as working memory; a sound
intermediate step makes the following ones easier to get right, and the prompt moves the model
into the register of worked solutions in its training data. (Section 9.1)

**3.** Zero-shot CoT simply adds an instruction such as "Let's think step by step" to the
prompt, with no examples. Few-shot CoT includes worked examples whose answers show the
intermediate steps; it is usually more reliable but requires crafting good examples.
(Section 9.1)

**4.** STRIPS (1971) formalized planning in terms of an initial state (a set of true
propositions), a goal (the propositions that should become true) and actions, each with
preconditions that must hold before it applies and effects that change the state. A plan is a
sequence of actions that transforms the initial state into the goal state, which makes the
plan the solution and the other three the problem's core components. (Section 9.2)

**5.** Advantages of LLM-based planning: it needs no hand-crafted action schemas, because the
model draws on its parametric world knowledge, and it scales to open-domain, novel tasks.
Disadvantages: it has no completeness or correctness guarantee, and it carries a high
hallucination risk, producing plans that read well but are wrong. (Section 9.2, Table 9.1)

**6.** The model generates a response, critiques it against stated criteria, revises it if
the criteria are not met, and repeats until they are met or an iteration limit is reached. It
improves output reliably only when the problem is one the critique can actually detect,
ideally with explicit, checkable criteria or external feedback; if the error comes from a flaw
the model cannot see, the same flaw affects generation and critique alike. The iteration limit
is essential, because an unbounded loop is a production failure mode. (Sections 9.3, 9.6)

**7.** Deliberation is extended thinking inside the generation process: an o1/o3-style model
first generates a hidden sequence of reasoning tokens, exploring alternatives and checking
intermediate results, and only then writes the visible answer. Chain-of-thought is a prompting
technique applied to a standard model, whose reasoning appears in the output; deliberation is
built into the model by training, happens before the answer, and is usually hidden from the
user or shown only as a summary. (Section 9.4)

**8.** Reasoning tokens are the tokens a reasoning model generates internally before its
visible answer. They are generated autoregressively and billed like output tokens, so a
response with 2,000 reasoning tokens and a 200-token answer costs about eleven times the
output of a direct 200-token answer and takes longer; for simple tasks that overhead is wasted.
(Sections 9.4, 9.7)

**9.** The generated code is run in a sandbox, usually against tests; if it fails, the error
or failing test output is appended to the context and the model regenerates the code, until it
passes or a retry limit is reached and the task is escalated. It is more reliable than
prompted self-correction because the judgment comes from an objective, external signal, the
execution result, not from the same model that made the error. (Section 9.6)

**10.** Any four from Section 9.8. Failure on novel problems is hard to fix because the
models rely on patterns resembling their training data. Compounding errors in long chains
persist because a locally coherent chain gives the model no signal that an early step was
wrong. Reasoning hallucination is difficult because well-structured, confident reasoning can
contain a false intermediate fact that looks no different from a true one. Cost and latency
follow directly from generating many extra tokens. The absence of formal guarantees means the
reasoning cannot be proved correct, so outputs still need external validation. (Section 9.8)

---

## Chapter 10 — Prompt Engineering Foundations

**1.** The chapter defines prompt engineering as designing, testing and iterating on inputs to
reliably produce desired outputs. "Writing prompts" is a single act judged by one good result;
prompt engineering is a systematic, empirical process that measures performance across the
full range of inputs, versions prompts like code, and continues after deployment, with
reliability, not a single success, as the standard. (Section 10.1)

**2.** The system prompt establishes the model's role, behavioral rules, capabilities and
default output standards for the whole interaction; the user message carries the immediate
request; context supplies the background information the model needs, such as documents,
records or conversation history; and assistant prefill, where supported, writes the start of
the model's response to steer its format or role. (Section 10.3)

**3.** Models use information near the beginning and end of a long context more reliably
than information in the middle. Place critical instructions and the most important context at
the beginning or end, keep context focused, and do not bury the key document among many
others. (Section 10.5, Table 10.3)

**4.** A strong answer uses action verbs, an explicit output type and resolved ambiguities, for
example: "Write a 120–150-word product description for the home page of our website. Audience:
small-business owners comparing project-management tools. Describe what the product does and
its three main benefits, using the feature list below. Use a friendly, professional tone, plain
language and no jargon. End with one sentence inviting the reader to start a free trial. Output
only the description, as two short paragraphs." (Section 10.4)

**5.** A format constraint governs the structure, length or presentation of the output, for
example "Respond in under 100 words" or "Return a JSON object with exactly these fields:
`title`, `summary`, `confidence`." A behavioral constraint governs how the model handles
situations, for example "Answer only questions about our products; for anything else, reply
that you can only help with product questions" or "If you are not confident, say so."
(Section 10.6)

**6.** Design, whose deliverable is the first version of the prompt; Test, a test suite of
diverse cases (at least 50) including edge and adversarial ones; Evaluate, a scorecard of
accuracy, format compliance, constraint adherence and hallucination rate; Iterate, new prompt
versions that fix failing cases without regressions; Deploy, the production prompt with
logging, a pinned model version, output validation and fallbacks; and Monitor, a quality
dashboard tracking behavior on production inputs and after model updates. (Section 10.8,
Table 10.5)

**7.** Prompt injection is user-supplied text that contains instructions intended to override
or circumvent the system prompt, such as "Ignore your previous instructions and…". It works
because the model processes all the text in its context and can treat untrusted text as
instructions. Defenses include separating user content structurally from instructions with
delimiters or tags, instructing the model to ignore instructions inside user content,
validating and sanitizing input at the application level, and treating all user-generated
content as untrusted. (Section 10.9)

**8.** It is hallucination: the model is producing plausible information that its source does
not support. The fix is to ground the answer in the document, instructing the model to answer
only from the provided text and to say when the document does not contain the answer, and to
verify outputs against the source where accuracy matters. (Section 10.9)

**9.** Assistant prefill writes the beginning of the model's response, which the model then
continues. It solves format and role problems, for example starting with `{` so the output is
JSON without a prose preamble, or starting with a heading to enforce a structure. Not every API
or model supports it. (Section 10.3)

**10.** Any two: programmatic prompts are built dynamically from templates whose variables
are filled from databases, APIs or user input, instead of typed by hand; constrained-generation
libraries enforce the output format at the token-sampling level; prompt chaining feeds one
prompt's output into the next; and the prompts themselves are treated as code, versioned,
tested and deployed through CI/CD pipelines. (Section 10.10)
